description: Milgram's Agency theory, social factors shaping obedience, and Adorno's Authoritarian Personality.
content_html:
What Is Obedience?

Obedience is when a person follows a direct instruction from someone they perceive to be in authority. Unlike conformity, which involves going along with a group without being told to, obedience involves a clear command from a perceived authority figure. Milgram’s work revealed just how powerful this influence can be.

Milgram’s Agency Theory

Milgram proposed the Agency theory to explain why people obey. He argued that humans shift between two psychological states depending on the social situation.

When a person is in an agentic state, they view themselves as an agent or instrument of an authority figure. They feel they are simply carrying out orders and pass the responsibility for any consequences upward to the person giving the instructions. This state increases obedience dramatically.

In contrast, when a person is in an autonomous state, they act independently and take personal responsibility for what they do. In this state, people are far more likely to resist instructions that conflict with their own values.

Key Fact

Milgram’s Agency theory states that people enter an agentic state when following an authority figure, passing responsibility upward and increasing obedience. In an autonomous state, people feel personally responsible for their actions and are more likely to resist.

Key Fact

Milgram’s (1963) Study of Obedience: Aim — to investigate whether ordinary people would obey an authority figure’s instruction to harm an innocent person. Method — 40 male American participants were told to administer electric shocks to a confederate ‘learner’ for wrong answers; shocks ranged from 15V to 450V in 30 increments of 15V; when participants hesitated, the experimenter used four verbal prods (“Please continue” through to “You have no other choice”). Results — 65% of participants (26 out of 40) administered the maximum 450V shock; all participants gave at least 300V. Conclusion — ordinary people will obey authority figures even when ordered to cause serious harm to others, supporting the idea that the agentic state overrides personal morality.

Social Factors Affecting Obedience

Milgram identified four key social factors that affect how much a person obeys: agency, authority, culture and proximity.

Authority affects obedience because people learn from an early age to respect those in positions of power such as doctors, teachers and police officers. The more legitimate and credible the authority figure appears, the more obedience is shown. In Milgram’s research, when the experimenter’s authority was made less clear — for example, by replacing them with an ordinary person — obedience dropped considerably.

Culture shapes how much people are taught to value obedience to authority. Different societies place different emphasis on compliance with rules and hierarchies. Research replicating Milgram’s design in other countries has generally found high levels of obedience, suggesting this is a widespread human tendency, though exact rates vary across cultures.

Proximity to the victim reduces obedience. When the person being harmed is nearby or visible, the reality of what is happening becomes harder to ignore and participants are more likely to resist. When the victim is physically distant — for example in another room — it is easier to remain in the agentic state and continue obeying. Milgram found that obedience fell when the ‘learner’ was in the same room as the participant.

Dispositional Factors: Adorno’s Authoritarian Personality

Not everyone obeys to the same degree. Adorno argued that some people have a personality type that makes them particularly prone to obedience. He called this the Authoritarian Personality.

People with an authoritarian personality tend to show great respect for authority figures while being hostile towards those they see as inferior or different. They prefer clear rules and rigid categories. Adorno linked this personality type to a strict, punitive upbringing where children learned to obey without question and to fear and resent those with less power. As a result, they displace their anxieties downward onto weaker groups while showing submission upward to those in authority.

Key Fact

Adorno’s Authoritarian Personality is a dispositional explanation of obedience: individuals with this personality type show high deference to authority and hostility towards out-groups, linked to a harsh, rule-bound upbringing.

Evaluating Agency Theory and the Authoritarian Personality

Agency theory has a strength in that it fits with Milgram’s own experimental evidence. When variations reduced the authority of the experimenter or increased the participant’s proximity to the victim, obedience fell — exactly as the theory would predict. This gives the theory empirical support.

A weakness of agency theory is that it does not easily explain why some individuals resist obedience even in the same agentic-state conditions. It treats the shift to the agentic state as relatively automatic, but many people do manage to disobey even under strong authority pressure, which the theory cannot fully account for.

Adorno’s Authoritarian Personality theory is criticised for relying heavily on case studies and self-report questionnaires, which may lack reliability and validity. It also presents obedience as a stable personality trait, which underestimates the powerful situational factors that Milgram’s work revealed. The two explanations — dispositional (Adorno) and situational (Milgram) — are best seen as complementary rather than competing.

Understanding both theories also has real-world applications. Milgram’s situational account suggests that obedience can be reduced by weakening the conditions that trigger the agentic state — for example, by making authority less legitimate, bringing people closer to the consequences of their actions, or encouraging individuals to take personal responsibility. Adorno’s dispositional account suggests that how people are brought up and taught to relate to authority also matters in shaping whether they will resist destructive orders.
exam_tip_html: On 9-mark questions about obedience, a common mistake is describing only the agentic/autonomous states and ignoring the four social factors (agency, authority, culture, proximity). Make sure you cover both the theory AND the factors. For evaluation, contrast Milgram’s situational explanation with Adorno’s dispositional one — this shows you understand the wider debate about why people obey.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Milgram’s Agency theory explains obedience through the shift from autonomous to agentic state — in the agentic state, responsibility passes upward to the authority figure, increasing compliance.
  • Social factors — authority, culture, proximity and the shift into the agentic state — all increase or decrease how much a person obeys.
  • Adorno’s Authoritarian Personality offers a dispositional complement: individuals who grew up with harsh, rule-bound parenting tend to show high deference to authority figures.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the agentic state?
A) Acting independently and taking personal responsibility
B) Being in a crowd and losing individual identity
C) Seeing oneself as carrying out the wishes of an authority figure
D) Changing behaviour to match a peer group
practice_questions.marks: C) Seeing oneself as carrying out the wishes of an authority figure [1 mark]
Obedience is following a direct order or instruction [1 mark] from a person perceived to be in a position of authority [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how proximity affects obedience according to Milgram's Agency theory.
practice_questions.marks: Proximity refers to physical or psychological closeness to the person being harmed [1 mark]. When the victim is nearby or visible, obedience decreases because the consequences of following orders become more vivid and harder to ignore [1 mark]. When the victim is in another room or out of sight, it is easier to remain in the agentic state and continue to obey [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A manager tells a new employee to write a misleading report. The employee knows it is wrong but follows the instruction. Using Milgram's Agency theory, explain why the employee might obey.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains two relevant concepts from agency theory linked precisely to the scenario (e.g. the employee has shifted into an agentic state, seeing themselves as carrying out the manager’s wishes and passing moral responsibility upward; the manager’s authority as a supervisor is a social factor that legitimises the instruction, increasing compliance).
Secure: One concept clearly explained and linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names agency theory or the agentic state but does not link clearly to the specific scenario details.
Emerging: Vague reference to authority or following orders without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Adorno's theory of the Authoritarian Personality as an explanation of obedience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains what the Authoritarian Personality is (high deference to authority, hostility to out-groups, rigid thinking), its origins in a strict punitive upbringing, and how it explains individual differences in obedience; accurate use of psychological terminology throughout.
Secure: Describes the main features of the personality type and links to obedience; may lack detail on origins.
Developing: Identifies the personality type and one or two features but does not develop the link to obedience or origins.
Emerging: Brief, inaccurate or very vague description.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Milgram's Agency theory of obedience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of agentic and autonomous states plus the four social factors (agency, authority, culture, proximity); evaluation includes at least two developed points with elaboration (e.g. empirical support from Milgram’s variations; weakness that it cannot explain why some resist; contrast with Adorno’s dispositional account).
Secure: Description of the states and most social factors; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Description of one state and one or two social factors; evaluation present but underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description of obedience or authority; evaluation is a single undeveloped point.

knowledge_checks.q: According to Milgram's Agency theory, what happens when a person enters the agentic state?
options: They become more resistant to authority
They take full personal responsibility for their actions
They pass responsibility to the authority figure and are more likely to obey
They rely on the group to decide what to do

knowledge_checks.q: Which dispositional explanation argues that a strict upbringing produces high deference to authority?
When the victim is physically close to the person obeying, _____ to the victim reduces obedience.
In the _____ state, a person acts independently and takes personal responsibility for their actions.
Match each concept to its description:
right: Seeing oneself as an instrument of authority, passing responsibility upward
Acting independently and taking personal moral responsibility
A personality type with high deference to authority and hostility to out-groups

flashcard_questions.a: Following a direct order from a person perceived to be in authority.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the agentic state in Milgram's Agency theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Seeing yourself as carrying out another's wishes, passing moral responsibility upward.
Acting independently and taking personal responsibility for your own actions.
The more legitimate the authority figure appears, the greater the level of obedience.

flashcard_questions.q: How does proximity to the victim affect obedience?
flashcard_questions.a: Obedience falls when the victim is nearby, making the consequences more vivid and harder to ignore.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Adorno call the personality type linked to high obedience?
What kind of upbringing does Adorno link to the Authoritarian Personality?
flashcard_questions.a: A strict, punitive upbringing where children learned to obey without question.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one strength of Milgram's Agency theory.
flashcard_questions.a: Supported by Milgram's variations — obedience fell when authority or proximity changed as the theory predicts.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of Adorno's Authoritarian Personality theory.
flashcard_questions.a: It underestimates situational factors — Milgram showed most people obey regardless of personality type.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four social factors affecting obedience in Milgram's Agency theory.

glossary_terms.definition: Following a direct order or instruction from an authority figure.
The explanation that people obey authority because they see themselves as agents carrying out someone else's wishes rather than acting independently.
A psychological state in which a person sees themselves as an instrument of another person's will, reducing their sense of personal responsibility.
A psychological state in which a person sees themselves as responsible for their own actions and makes their own moral judgements.
Physical or psychological closeness to the person being harmed, which makes the consequences of obedience more vivid and reduces compliance.
A personality type proposed by Adorno, characterised by strong deference to authority figures, rigid thinking, and contempt for those seen as inferior or different.
